ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Bladder cancer is a malignant tumor of the urothelium, most often urothelial carcinoma. Diagnosis relies on urine cytology and cystoscopic biopsy, and staging follows depth of invasion.

sections.p: Bladder cancer is a malignant proliferation of urothelial cells, diagnosed by visualizing a lesion on cystoscopy and confirming histology from a biopsy.

t.b: Does the urine contain malignant cells? Positive cytology suggests high‑grade carcinoma; negative does not rule out low‑grade disease.
What is the visual appearance and histology? Direct visualization confirms tumor and biopsy provides grade and depth.

sections.p: Staging uses the TNM system; the key clinical split is non‑muscle‑invasive (Ta, T1, CIS) versus muscle‑invasive (T2‑T4).

t.b: Is the tumor beyond the bladder wall? Detects muscle invasion (T2) and extravesical spread (T3‑T4).
What is the depth of invasion and grade? Determines stage and guides treatment.

sections.p: The strongest risk is exposure to aromatic amines, especially from tobacco smoke; occupational exposure to dyes and chemicals follows.
b: Chronic Schistosoma haematobium infection (especially in Africa)

sections.p: Patients usually notice painless gross hematuria; irritative voiding symptoms appear later or with advanced disease.
Imaging and endoscopic assessment define extent; urine tests aid detection and surveillance.

t.b: If unavailable, proceed directly to cystoscopy.
If CT not available, MRI pelvis can substitute.
Are malignant cells present? Positive suggests high‑grade disease; negative does not exclude low‑grade.

sections.p: Rapidly growing tumors can cause obstructive uropathy, anemia from chronic bleeding, and metastasis to bone or lung.
Treatment follows stage: non‑muscle‑invasive disease gets intravesical therapy; muscle‑invasive disease requires radical cystectomy or chemoradiation.
b: Intravesical BCG for high‑grade Ta/T1/CIS – stimulates local immune response
Radical cystectomy with urinary diversion for T2‑T4
Neoadjuvant cisplatin‑based chemotherapy improves survival in muscle‑invasive disease
Avoid nephrotoxic agents in patients with renal impairment

sections.p: Surveillance cystoscopy and urine cytology are essential because recurrence is common; smoking cessation dramatically lowers risk.
b: Cystoscopy every 3‑6 months for first 2 years
Counsel on smoking cessation and avoid occupational exposures

sections.p: Other causes of hematuria can mimic bladder cancer.
Certain tests may be falsely negative or positive.
b: Urine cytology often misses low‑grade tumors
BCG therapy can cause sterile pyuria that mimics infection

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid weight loss or bone pain
Signs of infection after intravesical therapy

faq.q: Why is smoking the biggest risk?
faq.a: Tobacco contains aromatic amines that are metabolized to DNA‑damaging compounds in the urothelium.
Early non‑muscle‑invasive disease can be cured with intravesical therapy; muscle‑invasive disease often requires surgery and systemic therapy.
An intravesical immunotherapy that triggers a local immune response to destroy residual tumor cells.

exam: Explain how the depth of invasion determines treatment choice in bladder cancer.
List the major modifiable risk factors and how they contribute to carcinogenesis.
Describe the surveillance schedule after a transurethral resection of a high‑grade T1 tumor.
